title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at median age across counties in Washington State, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably. Median age is a useful metric to policymakers, as it can be used in determining funding for state programs such as youth or senior programs.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:

my_variable <- "B01002_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                           estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                             <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Garfield County, Washington        52.6   4.3    8.17
 2 Wahkiakum County, Washington       54.8   2.2    4.01
 3 Columbia County, Washington        52.1   1.9    3.65
 4 Douglas County, Washington         38.4   1      2.60
 5 Skamania County, Washington        48.6   1      2.06
 6 Kittitas County, Washington        37.9   0.7    1.85
 7 Walla Walla County, Washington     38.3   0.6    1.57
 8 Whitman County, Washington         26.1   0.4    1.53
 9 Ferry County, Washington           52.8   0.7    1.33
10 Asotin County, Washington          45.5   0.6    1.32


Garfield County has the least reliable estimate, with a margin of error of 8.17%.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 3  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 6 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

count(county_data, reliability)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  reliability         n
  <chr>           <int>
1 High confidence    36
2 Low confidence      1
3 Moderate            2


Assuming that a high confidence lies with less than 3 percent MOE, 36/39 counties are classified as “High confidence”. Of the remaining three, just Garfield County is of Low confidence (>6% MOE). The two remaining counties are of moderate confidence.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                       myvarE myvarM   popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                       <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 53001 Adams County, Washington     29.2    0.3  20690    NA
2 53003 Asotin County, Washington    45.5    0.6  22424    NA
3 53005 Benton County, Washington    36.2    0.2 210224    NA
4 53007 Chelan County, Washington    40.4    0.4  79518    NA
5 53009 Clallam County, Washington   51.8    0.3  77593    NA
6 53011 Clark County, Washington     38.9    0.2 510516    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 3  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 6 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         36        214725.
2 Low confidence           1          2326 
3 Moderate                 2          4284.


The average population of high-confidence counties is significantly higher than that of low and moderate-confidence counties. Similarly, moderate-confidence counties have higher populations than low-confidence counties. Thus, there appears to exist a direct linear relationship between a county’s population and MOE confidence.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
As a result of high margins of error, we know the least about the least populous counties in Washington state: Garfield, Wahkiakum, and Columbia counties. Due to its high margin of error, Garfield County has a median age of 52.6 +/- 8.17%. This means that the actual median age of Garfield County is anywhere between 48.3 and 56.9. This is a very wide range, the reason of which comes from the way the ACS works in practice. The 5-year ACS (American Community Survey) is a survey run by the United States Census Bureau that samples approximately 3.5% of the US population per survey conducted. As this is a sample, smaller regions will have less respondents relative to more populous regions. For example, Grant County, WA (population 100,428) would have an approximate sample size of 3,515 people; this yields an MOE of 0.9%. By contrast, a much smaller county such as Columbia County, WA (population 3,996) would only have an approximate sample size of 140 people; this yields in an MOE of 3.6%. When less individuals are sampled overall across a geographic area, the overall result has increased sampling variability, increasing the overall margin of error. This can have downstream effects for policymakers: to not know with accuracy the median age of a county, for example, can result in incorrect funding for schools (hurting younger individuals) or senior support programs (older individuals).

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim?
text:
The question
According to reporting by Axios, the share of single-person households in Seattle more than doubled in the course of 5 years, from 17% in 2016 to 40% in 2021. The report utilized ACS (American Community Survey) 1-year data to determine this. Should this statistic be taken at face value?
In this analysis, I utilize the margins of error provided by the ACS to determine the accuracy of this claim.

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim?
text:
Reconstruct

my_state <- "WA"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variables <- c("B11001_008",  "B11001_001")

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim?
text:
Pulling the data

city_data_t0 <- get_acs(
  geography = "place",
  variables = my_variables,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2016,
  survey = "acs1"
)

city_data_t1 <- get_acs(
  geography = "place",
  variables = my_variables,
  state = my_state,
  year = 2021,
  survey = "acs1"
)
  
single_households_t0 <- city_data_t0[grepl("Seattle", city_data_t0$NAME) & city_data_t0$variable == "B11001_008", ]
total_households_t0 <- city_data_t0[grepl("Seattle", city_data_t0$NAME) & city_data_t0$variable == "B11001_001", ]
single_households_t1 <- city_data_t1[grepl("Seattle", city_data_t1$NAME) & city_data_t1$variable == "B11001_008", ]
total_households_t1 <- city_data_t1[grepl("Seattle", city_data_t1$NAME) & city_data_t1$variable == "B11001_001", ]

single_households_t0_percent <- single_households_t0$estimate / total_households_t0$estimate * 100
single_households_t1_percent <- single_households_t1$estimate / total_households_t1$estimate * 100

cat("2016 -- Single Households / Total Households: ", single_households_t0$estimate, " / ", total_households_t0$estimate, " = ", single_households_t0_percent, "%\n")

2016 -- Single Households / Total Households:  123240  /  319125  =  38.6181 %

cat("2021 -- Single Households / Total Households: ", single_households_t1$estimate, " / ", total_households_t1$estimate, " = ", single_households_t1_percent, "%\n")

2021 -- Single Households / Total Households:  140816  /  351650  =  40.04436 %


Already, we have a discrepancy. The article states that in 2021, the rate for single households in 2021 was 40%. This matches my finding. However, in 2016, the article claims a figure of 17%, less than half the rate that I found.
Let’s find our margins of error. Perhaps that could reveal a missing link?

# computing percentage rate & its margin of error
single_households_t0_percent_moe <- moe_prop(single_households_t0$estimate, total_households_t0$estimate, single_households_t0$moe, total_households_t0$moe) * 100
single_households_t1_percent_moe <- moe_prop(single_households_t1$estimate, total_households_t1$estimate, single_households_t1$moe, total_households_t1$moe) * 100
cat("2016 margin of error:", single_households_t0_percent_moe, "% ")

2016 margin of error: 1.688009 % 

cat("2021 margin of error:", single_households_t1_percent_moe, "% ")

2021 margin of error: 1.852954 % 

single_households <- data_frame(
  year = c(2016, 2021),
  percent_estimate = c(single_households_t0_percent, single_households_t1_percent),
  percent_moe = c(single_households_t0_percent_moe, single_households_t1_percent_moe),
)

# computing coefficient of variation and reliability flag
single_households <- single_households %>%
  mutate(
    cv = (percent_moe / 1.645) / percent_estimate * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE     ~ "Unreliable"
    ),
  )


p_2016 <- single_households %>%
  filter(year == 2016) %>%
  pull(percent_estimate)

p_2021 <- single_households %>%
  filter(year == 2021) %>%
  pull(percent_estimate)

moe_2016 <- single_households %>%
  filter(year == 2016) %>%
  pull(percent_moe)

moe_2021 <- single_households %>%
  filter(year == 2021) %>%
  pull(percent_moe)

se_2016 <- moe_2016 / 1.645
se_2021 <- moe_2021 / 1.645

change <- p_2021 - p_2016
se_diff <- sqrt(se_2016^2 + se_2021^2)
moe_diff <- 1.645 * se_diff

z <- change / se_diff

significant <- abs(z) > 1.645
cat("Is the change in percentage between 2016 and 2021 significant? ", significant)

Is the change in percentage between 2016 and 2021 significant?  FALSE


What does this tell us? Not only was there not a doubling in single households in Seattle, as claimed by Axios, there wasn’t even any statistical change! This claim is clearly unsupported.

library(ggplot2)
library(gt)


df <- data.frame(
  group = c("2016-2021"),
  mean_val = c(change),
  sd_val = c(moe_diff)
)

df_2 <- data.frame(
  group = c("2016", "2021"),
  mean_val = c(p_2016, p_2021),
  sd_val = c(moe_2016, moe_2021)
)

ggplot(df, aes(x = group, y = mean_val)) +
  geom_col(fill = "skyblue", alpha = 0.8, width = 0.6) + # Draw the bars
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_val - sd_val, 
                    ymax = mean_val + sd_val), 
                width = 0.2,                             # Width of error bar caps
                color = "grey30",                        # Line color
                linewidth = 0.8) +                       # Thickness of lines
  labs(title = "Percentage Change in Single Households Over Time", 
       x = "Time Period", 
       y = "Percentage Change in single households") +
  theme_minimal()







ggplot(df_2, aes(x = group, y = mean_val)) +
  geom_col(fill = "green3", alpha = 0.8, width = 0.6) + # Draw the bars
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_val - sd_val, 
                    ymax = mean_val + sd_val), 
                width = 0.2,                             # Width of error bar caps
                color = "grey30",                        # Line color
                linewidth = 0.8) +                       # Thickness of lines
  labs(title = "Single Households Percentage by Year", 
       x = "Year", 
       y = "Percentage of single households") +
  theme_minimal()







reliability_table <- single_households %>%
  mutate(
    cv = (percent_moe / 1.645) / percent_estimate * 100,
    dot = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "🟢",

    ),

title: Assignment 3: Verify the Claim?
text:
Adjudication
Outside of the primary claim examined, the article also makes a few other, relatively easy claims to verify using Census data.
“Nearly 49% of residents aged 20 and older in the Seattle-Bellevue-Tacoma metro area are single, with 49.4% of women and 48% of men unmarried, per 2019 to 2023 U.S. Census American Community Survey data.”

metro_areas <- get_acs(
  geography = "cbsa",
  variables = my_variables,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)
percent <- metro_areas[grepl("Seattle", metro_areas$NAME),][2,]$estimate / metro_areas[grepl("Seattle", metro_areas$NAME),][1,]$estimate

cat("Percent of singles: ", percent * 100, "%")

Percent of singles:  27.97649 %


Conclusion: Not supported.
“Statewide, 48% of adults are single, compared to the national average of 49%.”

state_single_rates <- get_acs(
  geography = "state",
  variables = my_variables,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

percent_statewide <- state_single_rates[grepl("Washington", state_single_rates$NAME),][2,]$estimate / state_single_rates[grepl("Washington", state_single_rates$NAME),][1,]$estimate

cat("Percent of singles: ", percent_statewide * 100, "%")

Percent of singles:  27.21947 %


Conclusion: Not Supported.
“Whitman County, home to Washington State University, leads the state in singles, with 60% of residents unmarried.”

county_single_rates <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = my_variables,
  year = 2023,
  state = my_state,
  survey = "acs5"
)

percent_county <- county_single_rates[grepl("Whitman", county_single_rates$NAME),][2,]$estimate / county_single_rates[grepl("Whitman", county_single_rates$NAME),][1,]$estimate

cat("Percent of singles: ", percent_statewide * 100, "%")

Percent of singles:  27.21947 %


Conclusion: Not Supported.

Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
Build a half-mile zone around every station and merge the circles into one shape. Remember your units.

  st_buffer(dist = 2640) %>%
  st_union()

Pick whole cookies: which tracts don’t touch the zone at all?

  st_filter(station_zone, .predicate = st_disjoint)

[1] 162


Cut the dough: what share of each tract’s area falls inside the zone?

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, covered_area)

  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(pct_covered = replace_na(covered_area / tract_area, 0) * 100)

The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}

text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}



Finding a table name
On a dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page, look for the API link. The table name is the word after FROM in the example query. To see what values a column takes before you filter on it, ask for a count in CSV format:

Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

How many burglaries fall in each tract?

A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,   # sq ft in a sq mile
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )

If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)

Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
#ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()
#ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(n_transitstops))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code

Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.

Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? Use your last plot.

Your answer: The feature that ultimately lowered CV RMSE the most across the model was the raw number of transit stops. Interestingly, including the log-transformed number of transit stop density as well lowered the CV RMSE much lower compared with only using either predictor, despite the two predictors’ multicollinearity. The reason for the effectiveness of the raw predictor is in its relation to transit access. As more transit stops exist in a census tract, there is a greater likelihood of more buses that come through; more frequent transit leads to higher use. What explains the log-transformed predictor in conjunction is less predictable. Perhaps having denser transit stop locations offsets overestimations among larger census tracts? This could explain why the final model has more of a residual-reducing effect on the outer, less dense suburbs of Philadelphia than in the denser inner suburbs. The predictor that disappointed me the most was bus shelter density: I would have thought that transit investment as such would lead to a measurable increase in commuter ridership. However, this predictor made the model worse - this could be because of the even geographic distribution of bus shelters outside of Center City. The log-transformed transit stop density feature has a coefficient of 1.946. This means that for every 1% increase in transit stop density within the census tract, the public transit commute-share percentage increases by 1.946%. Within the remaining residuals map, the main cluster left appears to be Southwest Philadelphia. The one thing I can think of unique to that area is that it features the frequent, fast trolleys that run below Center City, perhaps encouraging more transit trips than the transit stop data, which does not distinguish between transit types, would let on. To account for this, I would use the ACS variable B08303 - Travel Time to Work. The remaining error beyond that might be noise - the rest of the map does not have significant clusters of residuals.

check_na <- function(formula, df) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).")

}

# 10-fold CV RMSE, same folds every time
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
  fit$results$RMSE
}

# Each house's prediction from the fold where it was held out
cv_pred <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10,
                                        savePredictions = "final"))
  fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred)
}

# Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter.
socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) {
  where <- str_squish(where)
  q <- paste0("$where=", URLencode(where, reserved = TRUE), "&$limit=", limit)
  if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE))
  url <- paste0("https://data.cityofchicago.org/resource/", dataset, ".geojson?", q)
  tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".geojson")
  resp <- tryCatch(download.file(url, tmp, quiet = TRUE), error = function(e) e)
  if (inherits(resp, "error")) stop("Portal request failed. Open this URL in a browser to see why:\n", url)
  st_read(tmp, quiet = TRUE)
}  
# helper function for calculating moran's I
# takes in all_sales and list of predictors, uses k=8 for queen weight
# example on how to call it: moran_i_cv(all_sales, predictors2)
library(sf)
library(spdep)

moran_i_cv <- function(all_sales, predictors, k = 8) {
  train <- all_sales %>%
    filter(split == "train")
  
  formula <- reformulate(
    termlabels = predictors,
    response = "sale_price"
  )
  
  cv_predictions <- cv_pred(formula, train)
  cv_residuals <- train$sale_price - cv_predictions
  
  # Extract coordinates safely whether 'train' is an sf object or standard data frame
  if (inherits(train, "sf")) {
    coords <- st_coordinates(train)
  } else if (all(c("lon", "lat") %in% colnames(train))) {
    coords <- as.matrix(train[, c("lon", "lat")])
  } else {
    stop("`all_sales` must be an 'sf' object or contain 'lon' and 'lat' columns.")
  }
  
  neighbors <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = k))
  weights <- nb2listw(
    neighbors,
    style = "W",
    zero.policy = TRUE
  )
  
  result <- moran.test(
    cv_residuals,
    weights,
    zero.policy = TRUE
  )
  
  # Return the Moran's I statistic numeric value
  return(unname(result$estimate["Moran I statistic"]))
}

fetch_permits_page <- function(offset) {
  resp <- request(permits_url) |>
    req_url_query(
      `$select` = "id,permit_type,issue_date,latitude,longitude",
      `$where` = permits_where,
      `$order` = "id",   # a stable sort keeps page boundaries consistent between requests
      `$limit` = permits_page_size,
      `$offset` = offset
    ) |>
    req_retry(max_tries = 5) |>
    req_error(body = function(resp) resp_body_string(resp)) |>
    req_perform()

  rows <- resp_body_string(resp) |>
    jsonlite::fromJSON(simplifyVector = TRUE)
  if (length(rows) == 0) return(tibble())
  as_tibble(rows)
}

Build r5r street network
The street network comes from BBBike’s Chicago OSM extract (~100 MB, refreshed weekly), which covers lon −88.01 to −87.40 and lat 41.64 to 42.09. Every sale falls inside that box, so the statewide Illinois PBF (~350 MB) isn’t needed. The download is skipped if the file is already present, and r5r caches the built network next to it, so later runs only pay the build cost when the PBF changes.


Code
r5r_dir <- "data/r5r_chicago"
dir.create(r5r_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

pbf_url <- "https://download.bbbike.org/osm/bbbike/Chicago/Chicago.osm.pbf"
pbf <- file.path(r5r_dir, basename(pbf_url))
if (!file.exists(pbf)) {
  request(pbf_url) |>
    req_retry(max_tries = 3) |>
    req_progress() |>
    req_perform(path = pbf)
}

Driving isochrones from the Loop
Driving-time isochrones from downtown Chicago (41.883249, -87.630944) at the cutoffs in isochrone_cutoffs. Note that r5r car routing uses free-flow speeds, so congestion isn’t modelled.


Downtown drive time for each sale
Car travel time from downtown to each sale’s own coordinates, routed with travel_time_matrix(). This replaces looking each sale up in the isochrones: the isochrones are drawn from a coarse grid and have holes wherever a grid point can’t be reached by car, which left 19 sales with NA. Routing each sale snaps it to the nearest drivable road instead.


Code
downtown <- data.frame(id = "downtown", lat = 41.883249, lon = -87.630944)

# Many sales share coordinates, so route each unique location once.
# r5r needs an `id` column, which is renamed so it doesn't clash with all_sales$id
sale_pts <- all_sales |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  distinct(lon, lat) |>
  mutate(pt_id = as.character(row_number()))

downtown_tt <- travel_time_matrix(
  r5r_core,
  origins = downtown,
  destinations = rename(sale_pts, id = pt_id),
  mode = "CAR",
  departure_datetime = as.POSIXct("2023-10-04 08:00:00"),
  max_trip_duration = 90,
  progress = FALSE
)

all_sales <- all_sales |>
  select(-any_of("downtown_drive_time")) |>
  left_join(sale_pts, by = c("lon", "lat")) |>
  left_join(select(downtown_tt, pt_id = to_id, downtown_drive_time = travel_time_p50), by = "pt_id") |>
  select(-pt_id)

# LODES8 2023 Illinois OD, all jobs (JT00), all workers (S000). "main" keeps pairs where
# both home and work are in Illinois; lehdr caches the ~30 MB download.
lodes_args <- list(
  state = "il", year = 2023, version = "LODES8",
  lodes_type = "od", job_type = "JT00", segment = "S000",
  agg_geo = "block", state_part = "main", use_cache = TRUE
)

od_raw <- tryCatch(
  do.call(grab_lodes, lodes_args),
  error = function(e) {
    if (!grepl("outside the valid range", conditionMessage(e))) stop(e)
    # lehdr 1.2.0 hard-codes LODES8 years as 2002-2022 even though the 2023 release exists.
    # Reproduce what grab_lodes() does for that file: same URL, cache path and column types.
    message("lehdr rejected year 2023; downloading the LODES8 file directly instead")
    lodes_url <- "https://lehd.ces.census.gov/data/lodes/LODES8/il/od/il_od_main_JT00_2023.csv.gz"
    lodes_cache <- tools::R_user_dir("lehdr", which = "cache")
    dir.create(lodes_cache, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
    lodes_file <- file.path(lodes_cache, paste0("lodes8_", basename(lodes_url)))
    if (!file.exists(lodes_file)) {
      request(lodes_url) |> req_retry(max_tries = 3) |> req_perform(path = lodes_file)
    }
    read_csv(lodes_file, col_types = cols(w_geocode = "c", h_geocode = "c", createdate = "c")) |>
      mutate(year = 2023L, state = "IL")
  }
)

  select(w_geocode, h_geocode, year, S000) |>
  mutate(S000 = as.integer(S000))

Our final model fails the worst at predicting house prices that are actually very high, especially those near the Loop. The model is guessing too low. We think this is because it is more difficult to predict for the range of a “very expensive” house, which is much larger than that of an average-priced house. Moreover, we assumed that a fixed effect spatial feature (e.g. distance to the Loop) would not need to be included in our model because it would be collinear with other similar “spatial” features like downtown drive time, which would have reflected similar patterns. Our model’s ratio, with a median of 0.998 differs by neighborhood income. The maximum ratio is 67 which is very high - this indicates predicted price was way overpredicted of the actual sale price.
However the highest ratio of 67 means that those houses are over-valued. This means that lower-income neighborhoods face disproportionate property tax-burden compared to higher-income neighborhoods. Conversely, luxury homes in higher-income areas often sell at premium prices that standard linear models under-predict (ratios below 1.0, like the 1st quartile of 0.743), leaving wealthier homeowners under-taxed.
This imbalance mirrors the core finding of The Tax Divide. Algorithmic and traditional assessment models routinely over-assess low-value properties while under-assessing high-value properties, creating a regressive tax structure.
In part 1, we cleaned out houses that cost over around $1800 per square foot, houses less than $20,000 and houses over $10 million. When we examined the standard deviation for price per square foot in the training dataset, three standard deviations away from the mean was 1800. We cleaned out 5 upper outliers this way that seemed way too far from the rest of our data set to accurately contribute to the model. Filtering out the low-end sales under $20k created an artificial price floor forcing the model to over-predict low-income home values that were outside of our model range. Simultaneously, removing luxury outliers (>$1800/sqft and >$10m) capped top-end predictions which led to under-assessment in these high-income neighborhoods. By trimming these extreme data anchors, the cleaning actually caused regressivity across both ends of the income spectrum.

Your answer:
violentcrime_660ft: Holding all other structural, location, and quadratic terms constant, each additional violent crime reported within 660 feet of a home is associated with an estimated linear decrease of $3,694.90 in sale price.
If we were to hand this model in to the Assessor, we would warn them about a number of things.
(1) The model exhibits significant residual error and spatial bias. With an RMSE of $\$271,036$, individual property valuations can be off by hundreds of thousands of dollars. Furthermore, a Moran’s I of 0.270 indicates strong positive spatial autocorrelation, meaning the model’s errors are geographically clustered—it will systematically over-value or under-value entire neighborhoods rather than spreading errors randomly. Additionally, sparse extreme features create unrealistic coefficient swings (e.g., 12 bedrooms reducing predicted value by over $1.49M and 1 fireplace having a negative coefficient), making the model vulnerable to edge-case properties.
(2) There are many factors that influence a house’s sale price. We were able to explore many factors in this exercise through open-sources alone. However, there are a lot of proprietary datasets that are locked behind a paywall (i.e. GreatSchools for school ratings and performance). If the Assessor wants even further analysis done on predicting house sale prices, they may want to consider additional datasets.
(3) On the other hand, using too many factors could add unintended noise to the model. Given more time, we would test both more and fewer features to see their impact on our model.
